_comment: Shared contract for the canonical form, read by BOTH the Dart canonicalizer test and the Java
one. The two implementations exist so neither side's equality check depends on the other's code;
this file is what stops them drifting apart. A case added here must pass in both languages.
R1  bookkeeping about the message is dropped anywhere it appears: the write stamp, and
any key the underscore convention marks as protocol. A property name never starts with
one, so this can never remove state.
R2  a key whose value is a type default is dropped: null, false, numeric zero, empty array.
Both codecs elide those when writing, so absent and default-valued must compare equal.
R3  an empty string and an empty object are NOT dropped. A sender that writes one means
something by it, and the bias rule says report unequal when unsure.
R4  numbers compare by value: 1 and 1.0 are the same number.
R5  object keys are sorted; key order carries nothing.
R6  array order IS significant - it is child order - and arrays recurse elementwise.
The bias rule behind R3 and R7: a canonicalizer that normalises away a real difference produces
silent false greens across every probe that depends on it. One that reports a spurious
difference only costs someone a look. When a rule is arguable, it goes the strict way.

equal.why: R1 - the keys describing an update are not part of the state it updates
R1 - a differing write stamp is not a differing state
R2 - absent equals an empty list
R2 - defaults nested inside an object drop too
R1 + R2 together, nested in a child list

differ.why: R3 - an empty string is not an absent value
R3 - an empty object is not an absent value
a non-default value against a dropped default - the cross-language default hazard
a property present on one side only, with a real value
a missing child is not an equal tree
identity is state - the same shape under a different id is a different widget
a number is not its string
